Gnu Social and Diaspora are currently the popular OSS social networks, but they are a bad direction to be heading - everything is public in Gnu Social (fine for some people, but locks out or undermines any friends wanting privacy), and Diaspora is a silo written by people so incompetent it had no security in its first release, so security had to be bolted on as an afterthought instead of designed in... bolted on by already-incompetent people).

Hubzilla also has the killer feature of not tying your social network to any one website, this doesn't matter for facebook because you know the website will still be around in 10 years, but non-commercial social network websites are often volunteer run and not as dependable. Alright, now I'm really curious about Hubzilla. Do they distribute your account across various servers or do you host your own account?

You have an account on a hub you host yourself, or a friend of a mate hosts it, or you use one of the public Hubzilla servers.

You can roam to other websites with your identity(s), and set up other accounts on other websites with your identity (I think, I haven't tried that yet, I think there's an update button to pull a copy of your network of contacts into the new account) - but "magic auth" means you don't normally create accounts on other websites, the hub you're browsing will authenticate you automatically through your home website, no username or password required.

However, if your hub's about to go permanently offline, there's the separate issue of needing to export all your content (posts, photos, files etc), and upload it to the new home. It does this, but you'll be in a pickle if the website goes down before you get your stuff off it.

Hubzilla are trying to avoid being called social media, because the hubs don't need all your friends to be on the network in order to be useful - they have functionality and usefulness that's independent of that. This means it's quite hard to learn what Hubzilla actually is - all the descriptions are vague and abstract, but it already has everything that a social network has, plus it has bridges with other social networks which allow that.

I think you'll find Diaspora can no longer interact with Facebook, as FB have locked out most of that functionality (I say this so Hubzilla isn't dismissed for not having it - I get the impression Hubzilla put a lot more effort into standards and interoperability than Diaspora does)
